strengths: Introduces a novel, low-cost earphone-based ExG hardware prototype (NeuroBuds) enabling unobtrusive, long-term, free-living physiological data collection, which is a meaningful departure from bulky lab-based EEG headsets.
Contributes a new dataset, DailySense, with 50 hours of free-living recordings and 20 hours of labeled task-specific data spanning five human senses, filling a gap in ExG benchmark diversity.

The physiology-informed multi-band tokenization (PiMT) is a well-motivated and interpretable design choice, grounded in known physiological frequency bands, and is shown via ablation (1/2/4/12-band comparison) and saliency analysis to meaningfully improve performance.

Extensive empirical evaluation: results on DailySense plus four public benchmarks (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, BCI IV 2b), ablations on pretraining components and patch size, LOSO evaluation, cross-subject/cross-session generalization tests, and on-device efficiency analysis on a smartphone.

Consistent, non-trivial performance gains over strong baselines (PatchTST, Bidirectional-Mamba, EEGNet, etc.) both with and without pre-training, and demonstrated scalability of pre-training with more free-living data.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is limited: the DailySense dataset is not confirmed to be released (still "working with legal team"), and the earphone hardware is a custom prototype, making it hard for others to replicate the data collection or verify results.

Cross-subject generalization is weak (F1 drops from ~87.6% within-session to ~58.6% cross-subject), and in this setting PiMT even underperforms PatchTST on gaze regression, which undercuts the paper's core claim of learning robust, task-agnostic, generalizable representations.

Task-specific labeled subsets in DailySense are very small (up to only 7 participants per sense-specific task), raising concerns about statistical reliability and overfitting for the six downstream tasks.

The filter bank of 12 bands is fixed via heuristic physiological knowledge rather than learned or rigorously justified; some bands overlap in range (e.g., QRS complex 8–50 Hz vs. EEG-beta/gamma), and no ablation isolates the effect of the overlapping/redundant bands.

Comparisons on public benchmarks are restricted to only two strong baselines (PatchTST, Bidirectional-Mamba); more recent self-supervised EEG foundation models mentioned in related work (BIOT, BrainWave, LaBraM/large brain model) are not empirically compared, leaving the significance of gains vs. state-of-the-art self-supervised methods unclear.

The claim of a "task-agnostic" framework is somewhat overstated since the approach still requires task-specific fine-tuning and decoders per downstream task rather than truly zero-shot or unified multi-task inference.

Demographic diversity of the 22 participants is limited and skewed (16 men vs. 6 women, no discussion of other diversity factors), which may limit generalizability of the collected DailySense benchmark.

The reported improvements on public benchmarks (e.g., DREAMER, Sleep-EDF) are relatively modest in absolute terms and sometimes fall within overlapping standard deviations, weakening the strength of the generalization claim beyond DailySense.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel hardware prototype (NeuroBuds) for unobtrusive, low-cost, earphone-based multi-modal ExG (EEG/EMG/EOG) sensing, addressing a real gap between lab-grade and everyday wearable physiological sensing.

Contributes a new dataset (DailySense) with 50 hours of free-living recordings and 20 hours of labeled data spanning five human senses, which if released would be a valuable community resource; also validates signal quality against a research-grade OpenBCI device (0.71-0.76 correlation).

The physiology-informed multi-band tokenization (PiMT) is a well-motivated and interpretable design that decomposes signals into canonical frequency bands rather than relying on a single wide/narrow band, and is shown empirically to outperform 1/2/4-band variants as well as STFT/CWT tokenization.

Extensive and careful experimentation: results on DailySense and four public benchmarks (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, BCI-IV-2b), ablations on pre-training components and patch size, backbone comparison (Mamba vs Transformer), frozen-encoder evaluation, LOSO analysis, statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon), on-device latency/memory profiling, and comparison against pre-training on much larger public EEG corpora (TUAR/TUSZ).

Reasonably strong and consistent quantitative gains over multiple representative baselines (SVM, EEGNet, DeepConvNet, TST, PatchTST, EEGConformer, Bidirectional-Mamba) across diverse tasks, with saliency analysis providing some interpretability of which frequency bands drive each task.
weaknesses: The DailySense dataset, which is a core claimed contribution, is not released and its public availability is uncertain ("currently working with our legal team"), significantly weakening reproducibility and the paper's practical impact.

Cross-subject generalization is weak (F1 ~0.58-0.59 vs ~0.88 within-session in Appendix O/Table 12), which undercuts the paper's central claim of learning broadly generalizable, task-agnostic representations; this is acknowledged but somewhat downplayed in the main text.

Dataset scale remains modest (22 participants, as few as 6-9 per public benchmark, up to 7 per DailySense task), and demographic diversity is limited, raising concerns about the robustness and generalizability of the reported improvements.

The term "task-agnostic" is potentially overstated since the framework still requires task-specific fine-tuning (and separate decoders) rather than exhibiting true zero-shot/few-shot cross-task transfer; the encoder architecture (Bidirectional-Mamba) is also adopted directly from prior work rather than a new contribution.

Some of the 12 predefined frequency bands (e.g., ECG-LF/HF ranges borrowed from HRV literature) are applied to short 4-second windows, raising questions about their physiological validity/meaningfulness at this timescale that are not discussed.

Fair pre-training comparison is limited to PatchTST as the only baseline with a tailored pre-training strategy; other competitive baselines (e.g., EEGConformer, Bidirectional-Mamba without PiMT) are not evaluated with equivalent pre-training in the main results, making the size of the pre-training benefit somewhat one-sided in the comparison.
